MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
## Van name

Since it's a staff vote, here are a few to put on the ballot:
- **Dovetail**
- **Chester** (as in Chesterfield)
- **The French Polisher**
- **Vincent Van Go**
- **Old Faithful**

**Dovetail** is probably the strongest. It's a woodworking joint, it's friendly, and it suits a restorer.

## Tomorrow's route

**The order has to be B → A → C.** It's the only order that works:
- C can't take anything before 11:00, so it must come last.
- Going to A first would mean finishing there at 09:15 and reaching B at 09:40, after the shop opens.

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B, done 25 min before opening ✓ |
| 09:30 | Arrive A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A, inside the 09:00–10:00 window ✓ |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** while waiting for C to open ✓ |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C ✓ |
| 12:00 | Back at depot (45 min) ✓ |

**Warning: there is no slack at all.** He gets back at exactly 12:00, so if the C drop overruns by even a minute, or there's traffic on the way back, he'll be late. Some options:
- Ask C whether they'd accept 10:45. That would give him 15 minutes of spare time.
- Agree with whoever needs the van at 12:00 that a few minutes late is fine.
- Make sure C has someone ready to receive at exactly 11:00.

The break fits neatly into the wait before C, so it costs him no time.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [20] minutes. See you soon!

If you need to make sure someone is home, add: "If you're not going to be in, please let us know on [number]."

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition:** check for new scratches, dents or marks on the finish, compared with the photos taken before it left the workshop.
2. **Completeness and function:** all parts are there (shelves, keys, handles, feet), and doors and drawers open and close smoothly.
3. **Customer sign-off:** the customer looks it over and signs, with any concerns written down there and then.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

Use an **emailed note as standard**, ideally signed on the driver's phone and sent with a photo of the delivered piece. It's timestamped, can't be lost, and gives you a clear record if there's a dispute. Keep **paper copies in the van** for customers who prefer them. Some of your restoration customers may well be people who'd rather have something in their hand.

## Proof of delivery (for the part-timer)

**Proof of delivery is the signed (or photographed) record showing the item arrived, when, who received it, and what condition it was in.**

## Evening-before text (142 characters)

> Hi Sarah, it's Oakwood Restorations. Your furniture is due tomorrow, 9-10am. We'll text when the driver sets off. Questions? Call 01234 567890

That's 142 characters with these sample details. Long customer or business names will push it up, so keep the total under 160.

Two technical points:
- **Use plain characters only.** A curly apostrophe (’), an en dash (–) or an emoji switches most phones to a different encoding, which cuts the single-message limit to **70 characters**. Your text would then split into several messages. Type a straight apostrophe (') and a plain hyphen (-), and watch out for apps that auto-convert them.
- **Give each drop its own window.** Based on tomorrow's plan: B "8:45-9:15am", A "9:15-10am", C "after 11am".
